content.prompt:
Consider the statement $P(n)$:
$$2^0+2^1+2^2+\cdots+2^{n-1}=2^n-1$$
for integers $n\geq 1$.
An attempted proof of this statement by induction is given below.
Proof:
Assume the statement is true for $n=k+1$.
That is,
$$2^0+2^1+2^2+\cdots+2^{k-1}+2^k=2^{k+1}-1 \qquad (1)$$
Next, we shall show it is true for $n=k$ by noting that if
$$2^0+2^1+2^2+\cdots+2^{k-1}+2^k=2^{k+1}-1$$
is true, then
$$2^0+2^1+2^2+\cdots+2^{k-1}+2^k=2\times 2^k-1$$
$$2^0+2^1+2^2+\cdots+2^{k-1}+2^k=2^k+2^k-1$$
Now subtracting $2^k$ from both sides of this equation, we have
$$2^0+2^1+2^2+\cdots+2^{k-1}=2^k-1$$
Which is true by statement (1).
Therefore, by the principle of induction, the statement $P(n)$ is true.
Give two reasons why the given proof is incorrect and does not prove $P(n)$.

answer.short: 1) No base case (e.g. n = 1) is shown. 2) The induction step is in the wrong direction: it assumes P(k+1) and tries to prove P(k), instead of assuming P(k) and proving P(k+1).
answer.worked:
Reason 1 (base failure): the proof never verifies a starting case such as n = 1. Without a base case, induction has nothing to start from, even if the implication were valid.

Reason 2 (reversed implication): the proof assumes P(k+1) and deduces P(k), that is, it shows P(k+1) implies P(k). Induction requires the forward implication: assume P(k) and prove P(k+1). The resulting $P(k)$ follows from the assumed $P(k+1)$, but it does not establish the forward implication required for induction.

These are two separate faults: the missing base case concerns the start of the chain, and the reversed step concerns the direction of the implication. Hence the argument does not prove P(n).

Test $n=1$:

$$\begin{aligned}f(k+1)-f(k)&=(3k+4)7^{k+1}-1-[(3k+1)7^k-1]\\&=3k\times7^{k+1}+4\times7^{k+1}-1-[3k\times7^k+7^k-1]\\&=21k\times7^k+28\times7^k-1-3k\times7^k-7^k+1\\&=18k\times7^k+27\times7^k\\&=9(2k\times7^k+3\times7^k)\\&=9Q.\end{aligned}$$

&=9(2k\times7^k+3\times7^k)\\
&=9Q,\text{ where Q is an integer}
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(f(k+1)-f(k)\) is divisible by 9 and \(f(k)\) is divisible by 9,
